notes.summary: This topic checks judgement rather than memory: how you act on duty, handle your own emotions, get along with people and think clearly about claims and rules. In most questions three options are clearly poor (ignoring the problem, losing temper, breaking rules, blaming others) and one is calm, fair, lawful and actually solves the problem. Logic and rule questions have exact answers, so check every condition.

concepts.title: How these questions are marked
concepts.body:
There is one best answer, chosen because it is the most responsible, balanced and effective. Ask of each option:
  • Does it solve or reduce the problem?
  • Is it legal, fair and honest?
  • Is it calm and respectful?
  • Does it follow the proper channel (senior, rules, police, helpline)?
The best option usually says yes to all four.

concepts.title: Options to reject
concepts.body:
• Doing nothing or "it is not my concern".
  • Shouting, insulting, threatening or taking revenge.
  • Breaking a rule to help someone, or accepting a favour or bribe.
  • Gossiping, complaining to others instead of the right person.
  • Quitting, giving up or blaming luck, teachers or the system.
  • Extreme steps: suspending everyone, stopping all work.

concepts.title: Emotional intelligence
concepts.body:
Emotional intelligence means understanding and managing your own feelings. It has five parts:
PartWhat it looks like
Self-awarenessKnowing what you feel and why
Self-controlStaying calm under pressure or criticism
MotivationLearning from failure and trying again
EmpathyUnderstanding how others feel
Social skillHandling relationships and disagreements well
The right answer stays calm, accepts feedback, learns from mistakes and talks things through in private.

concepts.title: Social intelligence
concepts.body: Social intelligence means understanding other people and working well with them. Pick options that include others, listen to both sides, give credit, share information and settle disputes fairly. As a leader, the best answer listens, decides on the basis of the goal and explains the reason.

concepts.title: Situation reaction on duty
concepts.body:
When you are put in an official role, follow this order of priority:
  1. Safety of human life comes first (accident, fire, medical emergency).
  2. Follow the law and the rules of the office; report wrongdoing to the proper authority.
  3. Be fair and transparent; no favours, no bias.
  4. Help the public, especially the poor or confused, within the rules.
Example: a poor villager hands in an incomplete form. Best: explain what is missing and help them complete it, not reject it silently or bend the rules.

concepts.title: Critical thinking
concepts.body:
• Fact or opinion: a fact can be checked; an opinion uses words like best, should, beautiful.
  • Definitely true means true in every case. "All trained staff got a bonus; Ravi got a bonus" does not prove Ravi was trained.
  • Reverse rule: from "If A then B", you may conclude "If not B, then not A". You may not conclude "If B, then A".
  • Strengthen or weaken: look for the option that directly supports or attacks the link between the reason and the claim.
  • Strong argument: important, directly linked to the question and based on a clear result.

concepts.title: Rule-based decisions
concepts.body:
Make a checklist of every condition, then tick each one for the case.
  • If every condition is met, the person qualifies.
  • If one condition fails, the person does not qualify, even if all the others are met with room to spare.
  • Watch boundaries: "between 18 and 28 years" and "at least 60%" include the end values unless the rule says otherwise.

concepts.title: Quick arithmetic
concepts.body:
Some reasoning papers include short arithmetic problems. Use the quant shortcuts:
  • Percentage: if 80% is spent, 20% is saved; saving ÷ 20% gives income.
  • Ratio: split a sum in the ratio a : b as sum × a/(a + b) and sum × b/(a + b).
  • Unitary method: more machines, fewer days (inverse); more hours, more work (direct).
  • Speed in km/h = metres per second × 18/5.

varieties.name: Situation reaction (on duty)
varieties.how: Put life and safety first, then the law and rules, then fairness. Reject options that ignore, delay or break rules.

example.q: You are a front-desk officer in a government building and the fire alarm rings. What should you do first?
steps: Safety of people comes first, before files or finding the cause.
Panicking or running out alone helps nobody; ignoring the alarm is unsafe.
Guiding visitors calmly to the exits, as per the evacuation plan, protects everyone.
example.answer: Calmly guide visitors to the nearest exit following the evacuation plan

varieties.name: Emotional intelligence
varieties.how: Choose the response that stays calm, accepts the feeling, learns from it and deals with the issue privately and constructively.

example.q: Your manager criticises your report in front of the team. What is the best response?
steps: Arguing in the meeting or sulking would show poor self-control.
Ignoring the feedback means you do not improve.
Listening calmly, noting the points and discussing them privately later shows self-control and a wish to improve.
example.answer: Stay calm, note the points and discuss improvements with the manager later

varieties.name: Social intelligence
varieties.how: Pick the option that includes people, listens to all sides and keeps the group working together.

example.q: A new teammate from another state does not speak the local language well and is left out of team discussions. What should you do?
steps: Leaving it to the manager or ignoring it keeps the teammate isolated.
Using a common language in meetings and helping the person settle includes them and helps the team.
example.answer: Use a language everyone understands and help the new teammate join in

varieties.name: Critical thinking and logic
varieties.how: Separate what must be true from what might be true. From "If A then B" you can conclude "not B, so not A", never "B, so A".

example.q: All students who scored above 90 got a scholarship. Meena did not get a scholarship. What is definitely true?
steps: Meena has no scholarship, so she cannot have scored above 90 (if she had, she would have one).

varieties.name: Eligibility and rule-based decisions
varieties.how: List every condition, tick each one for the case, and reject the case if even one condition fails.

example.q: Rules for a data-entry post: passed class 12 with at least 60% marks; typing speed of at least 40 words per minute; age 18 to 28 years. Raj passed class 12 with 65%, types 38 words per minute and is 22. Is Raj eligible?
steps: Typing: 38 is less than 40. Not met.
example.answer: No, Raj is not eligible because his typing speed is below 40 words per minute

varieties.name: Quick arithmetic puzzles
varieties.how: Turn the words into one simple equation and use the quickest quant shortcut.

example.q: A person spends 80% of his income and saves ₹2,000. What is his income?

tips: First cross out options that ignore the problem, lose temper, or break rules.
Life and safety come before property, paperwork or rules about timings.
Report wrongdoing through the proper channel, not through gossip or social media.
The best answer is usually calm, fair and active: it does something useful now.
In logic questions, "definitely true" means true in every possible case.
For eligibility, one failed condition is enough to reject a case.
traps: An option that sounds kind but bends the rules (letting a friend skip the queue) is wrong.
From "If A then B" and "B is true", you cannot conclude A.
Avoid options that pass the problem to someone else when you can act yourself.

questions.q: In a meeting, your colleague presents your work as his own. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Shout at him in front of everyone
Talk to him calmly in private, and inform the manager with facts if needed
Stop working with him for ever
Say nothing but complain about him to others
questions.solution:
Shouting or gossip harms everyone and avoiding him does not fix the problem.
A calm private talk, with facts shared with the manager if needed, protects your work and keeps the relationship professional.

questions.q: A new student in your class sits alone during lunch every day. What should you do?
options: Ignore the student; it is not your concern
Tell others that the student is unfriendly
Invite the student to join your group
Wait for the teacher to do something
questions.solution:
Including a newcomer is the socially intelligent choice.
Inviting the student helps them feel welcome; the other options leave them isolated.

questions.q: All employees who completed the training received a bonus. Ravi received a bonus. Which of the following is definitely true?
options: Ravi completed the training
Ravi may or may not have completed the training
Ravi did not complete the training
Only Ravi received a bonus
questions.solution:
The rule says: training → bonus. It does not say bonus → training.
Others may get a bonus for other reasons.
So Ravi may or may not have completed the training.

questions.q: You fail an important exam despite working hard. Which is the most emotionally intelligent response?
options: Decide that exams are unfair and stop preparing
Blame your teachers for the result
Analyse your mistakes and make a better plan for the next attempt
Pretend it does not matter to you
questions.solution:
Accepting the result and learning from it is a mature response.
Blaming others, quitting or hiding feelings does not help improvement.

questions.q:
Question: Should mobile phones be banned inside classrooms?
Arguments:
I. Yes, phones distract students during lessons.
II. No, all students like to have their phones.
options: Only argument I is strong
Only argument II is strong
Both arguments are strong
Neither argument is strong
questions.solution:
I is directly linked to learning in class and is important: strong.
II is based only on what students like, not on any real benefit: weak.
Only I is strong.

questions.q: You lead a team. Two members strongly disagree about how to finish a project, and the deadline is near. What is the best action?
options: Pick the plan of the senior member without discussion
Let them argue until one gives up
Listen to both, compare the plans against the goal and deadline, decide, and explain the reason
Do the whole project yourself
questions.solution:
A good leader hears both sides, decides on clear criteria and explains the decision.
This solves the conflict fairly and keeps the team working together before the deadline.

flashcards.back: No. Reversing the rule is a common logical error.
Relevant, important and directly linked to the question; not based on likes or popularity.
Calm, fair, solves the problem, respects everyone.
